How Production Loss Could Spread Across New Zealand Farms

A practical account of the scenario and its results

The story this model tells

This analysis asks a practical question: if a harmful event begins on a small number of farms, how far could it spread and how much production could be lost? It follows the real farm locations and attributes supplied in data/farms.csv.

The current population contains 150 farms. Each dot on the map is one of those farms. Its location, region, production type, shelter category and production capacity stay the same in every scenario. Production type is used to describe the results. Shelter also changes the modelled chance of a farm being reached.

At the start of a scenario, every farm is unaffected. The event begins at 3 selected farms and the model follows the next 60 days. A farm can be reached, spend time in an incubation period, become able to affect other farms, and finally have its production counted as lost. Nearby farms are more likely to be reached than distant farms, although the outcome still includes chance.

Why the scenario is repeated

One run gives only one possible chain of events. This analysis repeats the whole scenario 500 times over the same farm population. The starting locations and the chance outcomes can differ from one run to the next. Looking across all runs shows which outcomes are common and which sit at the more severe end of the range.

More runs make the pattern steadier, but they do not make the assumptions more realistic. The value of the results still depends on the farm data and the settings used.

The production base used in every scenario

The simulation starts from the same national production base in every run. The table provides context before any loss is modelled. The farm-level figures describe how capacity is distributed across farms; they are not simulation results.

The Grand total row gives the full capacity at risk. Its average, median and ranges describe individual farms across the complete input population.

What happened across the whole farm population

Each bar represents one possible national outcome. The orange share is production lost and the grey share is production remaining. A bar that is 80% orange means that scenario ended with 80% of national capacity lost. The two panels use the same percentage scale. Comparing their orange areas shows how the culling response shifts the range of national outcomes. The sorting is done separately in each panel, so bars in the same horizontal position are not necessarily the same matched run.

Across the repeated scenarios, average total loss was 124,477 birds, about 83.1% of the fixed population’s production capacity. Nine out of ten scenarios finished between 113,674 and 149,847 birds lost.

This is a widespread-loss result under the current settings. The average is useful for a central planning case, while the upper end of the range shows what a more severe outcome could look like. Because loss is already high in most runs, moderate changes to protection may be difficult to distinguish unless the spread and timing settings are well supported by evidence.

What changes when culling is used

The analysis also repeats every scenario with a culling response. This is a fair comparison: the no-control and culling versions begin at the same farms and use the same prepared chance values. The only intended difference is the response.

The current policy reaches 80% of active farms, then culls each covered farm 1 day after it becomes active. There is no separate daily limit: once the response delay has passed, every identified farm is culled.

Without control, average total loss was 124,477 birds. With culling, average total loss was 34,239 birds. That culling total already includes about 27,167 birds removed directly through culling.

After counting that direct loss, the response avoided an average of 90,238 birds, or 72.5% of the no-control loss. Total loss was lower with culling in 99.8% of the matched scenarios. The average number of affected farms fell from 124.1 to 34, while an average of 27 farms were culled.

This result shows the trade-off clearly. Culling accepts a smaller, immediate production loss to prevent a much larger chain. It does not mean this exact result would occur in practice. The benefit depends on finding active farms, reaching 80% coverage, acting within 1 day. Those assumptions should be tested against realistic response capability.

How the result differs by production type

Production type does not change how the event spreads in this model. It is used to show where the production consequences fall. A category with more farms or more capacity will generally have a larger total loss.

What the shelter comparison says

Sheltered survival averaged 16.5%, compared with 18% for unsheltered farms. The difference was -1.4 percentage points under the configured assumptions.

In these results, sheltered farms have a slightly lower raw survival rate. This does not mean shelter causes harm. The sheltered farms may simply be in more exposed places or may have been chosen as starting farms more often. The chart describes this farm population; it does not prove what shelter caused.

The cleanest future test would compare the same farms and the same starting conditions twice: once with shelter protection and once without it. That would separate the modelled shelter effect from differences in farm location.

Where the exposure sits

The left map shows the no-control result and the right map shows the matched culling result. Both bring the two islands into one view. Each bubble is one farm at its fixed location, and larger bubbles have more production capacity. Because the colour scale is shared, the two panels can be compared directly.

In the no-control panel, colour shows how often a farm reached the lost state through the normal modelled chain. In the culling panel, a farm is also counted as lost when it is culled. This is important: a coloured farm on the right may represent an early, deliberate loss that helped prevent many other farms from being reached.

For example, a value of 40% means that the farm reached the lost state in 40 out of every 100 simulated scenarios under the current settings and starting location method. It does not mean the farm is certain to lose 40% of its own production, and it is not a forecast that an event will occur. It is a scenario-based exposure measure: a high value identifies a farm that is often reached when many possible cascades are tested.

For example, 40% means the farm was counted as lost in 40 out of every 100 modelled scenarios for that panel. It does not mean that the farm loses 40% of its own production, and it is not a forecast that the event will occur. A high value simply marks a farm that is frequently exposed under the chosen settings and starting method.

Across all farms, the average lost-state probability falls from 82.7% without control to 22.6% with culling. On average, farms are directly culled in 18% of scenarios. The right panel should therefore be read as a mix of farms removed by policy and the smaller chain that continues despite that response.

The supporting farm-risk CSV also records how often each farm started a scenario, how often it was affected, how often it was lost, and its expected contribution to total loss. In random-start mode, some farms will be selected as starting points more often than others just by chance. The current setup selects each farm about 10 times on average.

Why the North Island looks more exposed

In the current results, the average chance of reaching the lost state is 97.6% for North Island farms and 37.2% for South Island farms. The main reason is how the scenarios begin.

There are 113 North Island farms and 37 South Island farms in the fixed population. With 3 starting farms chosen at random, at least one North Island farm starts the event in about 98.6% of runs. The South Island receives a starting farm in about 57.5% of runs.

The cross-island setting is currently 0, so an event cannot move from one island to the other. If a run has no South Island starting farm, every South Island farm stays unaffected in that run. The larger North Island population therefore gives the North Island many more opportunities to be involved.

This should not be read as proof that North Island farms are naturally more vulnerable. It is mainly a result of the number and location of farms, random starting points, and the blocked island crossing. The shelter shares are also fairly similar—47.8% in the North Island and 45.9% in the South Island—so shelter mix is not the main explanation here. These figures will update automatically when the full farm population is loaded and the analysis is rerun.

What happens between the islands

The farm data identify which island each farm belongs to. Farms on the same island have no extra barrier. For farms on different islands, the model applies the cross-island setting after allowing for distance and shelter.

The current value is 0. A value of 0 blocks spread between islands. A value such as 0.05 leaves a small cross-island pathway, while 1 removes the extra island penalty but still allows distance to reduce spread. A value above 0 should only be used when there is a credible route, such as ferry movements, shared equipment or supplier links.

The grey New Zealand shape and optional regional lines are there to make the map easier to read. They do not change the model.

What to take from these results

Under the current settings, the main message is that loss is widespread in most scenarios. The range across runs matters because it shows that the final loss is not fixed, even when the farm population stays the same. The map then adds the local view by showing which farms are repeatedly exposed.

These results are best used to compare plausible settings and identify where better evidence is needed. Straight-line distance cannot represent every real pathway. Animal movements, staff, vehicles, shared equipment, wind, cleaning practices and response actions may all change the real pattern. The model should support discussion, not replace operational judgement.

Running the analysis again

Start with the complete farm table in data/farms.csv. If its column names change, update the mappings in config.json. Choose how starting farms are selected, review the timing, distance, shelter, island and run settings, then run source("spatial_cascade_monte_carlo.R"). The refreshed charts and tables will be written to assets/. Finish by running quarto render spatial_cascade_report.qmd to rebuild this report.

Appendix: How timing and distance shape spread

The two parts of the model work together. Timing controls when a farm can spread. Distance controls how likely it is to reach another farm while it is active.

The left panel begins when a farm is reached. It spends 4 days incubating and cannot spread during that period. It then becomes active for up to 8 days. Without control, it moves to lost production at the end of that active period. If the farm is covered by the culling policy, it is culled 1 day after becoming active and can no longer spread. Coverage still matters: only 80% of active farms are selected for that response under the current settings.

The right panel begins with one active farm and one unaffected farm. At short distances, the model gives that transmission opportunity a higher chance. The chance falls smoothly as distance increases. Shelter lowers the whole curve for a sheltered farm. The different-island curve also includes the island setting; with the current value of 0, it stays at zero because cross-island spread is blocked.

This curve describes one opportunity from one active source. When several active farms can reach the same farm on the same day, the model combines those opportunities, so the farm’s overall chance of being reached can be higher than one line alone suggests.
